abstract: Gene flow is expected to homogenize populations, yet adaptive divergence can persist across environmental gradients. We investigated how genomic architectures and physiological tolerance shape salinity adaptation and resilience by combining whole-genome pool-sequencing of 11 copepod populations (Acartia tonsa) with common-garden physiology and dispersal modelling. Divergence between the high-salinity North Sea and low-salinity Baltic Sea was driven by few strongly differentiated genomic regions, while adaptation along the Baltic salinity gradient persisted despite gene flow and was highly polygenic, with candidate loci enriched for osmoregulatory processes. In common gardens, low-salinity populations survived reduced salinity better, corroborating genomic signals. Genomic offsets failed to capture range restrictions predicted by physiology-informed distribution models, likely because salinity tolerance behaves as a threshold trait, most impactful at range margins. Accounting for local adaptation reduced predicted habitat loss by 79%. Our results demonstrate that integrating physiological thresholds with genomics can improve forecasts of species' responses to environmental change.
